t: #3329 Count Substrings With K-Frequency Characters II
o: Count substrings of s in which some character occurs at least k times. Counting these directly is awkward, so invert: count the complementary 'bad' substrings where every character appears at most k−1 times, and subtract from the total n(n+1)/2. Bad substrings are exactly those captured by a classic at-most sliding window. For s='abacb', k=2: total 15, bad 11, answer 4.
k: Complement counting: good = total − bad, where bad means all frequencies ≤ k−1.
Bad substrings form a hereditary family (substrings of bad substrings are bad), so a two-pointer window counts them in O(n).
With only 26 letters, frequency updates are O(1); the window never needs per-step rescanning.

a.i: For each right endpoint r, shrink the left pointer until the window is bad (no frequency ≥ k); then every substring starting at l or later and ending at r is bad, contributing r−l+1. Summing gives the bad count.
s: Maintain cnt[26] and left pointer l = 0, bad = 0.
Extend r; increment cnt of s[r].
While cnt[s[r]] ≥ k, decrement cnt[s[l]] and advance l.
Add r−l+1 to bad; finally return n(n+1)/2 − bad.
a.t: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window at most once; O(26) work per step.

w: This single approach is optimal; mention the complement trick explicitly since it is the whole idea. Verify k = 1 (every non-empty substring is good → answer n(n+1)/2) and k > n (answer 0). Beware 64-bit counts: the answer can reach ~4.5×10^10. Follow-up: count substrings where every character appears at least k times, or at least m distinct characters each ≥ k.
